Plan: bring DrWrinch in line with the paper as of 2026-10-19

Source: PLAN_decision_rule.md

Written 2026-10-27 by Claude for Jake, in this repository.

Status at the end of 2026-10-27: the package changes below are made, in DrWrinch 0.0.2.1 (commit f3c04a8), which is on GitHub and on shinyapps.io. The edits to the paper repository are not made. The sections from “What changed in the paper” through “Decisions” describe the package as it stood before the update.

DrWrinch was last updated on 2026-08-29: version 0.0.2.0, commit e551b80, already pushed to GitHub. Since then the paper (~/repos/fully_specified_bf, last commit c93870c on 2026-10-19) has changed its rule for setting the rival aside, added two computations the package lacks, re-coded one application, and added a finite-archive version of both Bayes factors. Most of what the package has to do in response follows from the paper with no choice left open. Three choices about the package’s interface were left open, and the section “Your answers, 2026-10-27” records how you settled them.

What changed in the paper

The rule for setting the rival aside now has two thresholds

When the package was last updated, the authors claimed for the worst-case Bayes factor an error rate of at most one in twenty at a threshold of 20. The authors now state a different rule (Paper/evalues.qmd, section “Using the two Bayes factors to make a decision”): the researcher sets the rival aside when the uniform-weights Bayes factor is 20 or more and the worst-case Bayes factor is above 1. At nine observations for the working theory and three for the rival, both conditions hold, because 20.67 is at least 20 and 2.73 is above 1. The error-rate theorem is still in the supplement, but the authors no longer rest the main paper’s rule on it.

No function in the package computed whether this rule held, and three places followed the old rule:

  • sens_binomial() returned the search bias at which the uniform-weights Bayes factor falls below 20. It returned nothing about the worst-case Bayes factor.
  • sens_coding(model = "worst_case") returned a table of separations g*g^*, one row per re-coding. The supplement has commented that table out (Paper/appendix.qmd, lines 1157–1186). The main paper still computes g*g^* in one code chunk but no longer mentions it in its text.
  • The Shiny app applied one threshold to both Bayes factors. Its panel for the worst-case Bayes factor said that a researcher who sets the rival aside at the typed threshold is misled “at most one time in twenty,” whatever threshold was typed. The guarantee at a threshold tt is one time in tt, so at the paper’s threshold of 1 it promises nothing.

Both sensitivity analyses now ask when either condition fails

The authors write ω⋆\omega^\star for the smallest search bias at which the researcher would no longer set the rival aside: either the uniform-weights Bayes factor has fallen to 20 or the worst-case Bayes factor has fallen to 1, whichever happens at the smaller bias (Paper/evalues.qmd, sec-sensitivity, and the function omega_star() in the paper’s tests/bf_weighted.R). The worst-case condition needs the worst-case Bayes factor under a biased search, which Daniel added on 2026-10-01 as worst_bf_weighted(). A search with bias ω\omega turns a share θ\theta of the evidence into a share ωθ/(ωθ+1−θ)\omega\theta/(\omega\theta + 1 - \theta) among the observations found. The uniform-weights Bayes factor already used that tilt. Daniel’s function applies the same tilt and evaluates the rival at a share of one half in the evidence, which the search turns into a share of ω/(1+ω)\omega/(1 + \omega) among the observations found.

At nine of twelve the uniform-weights Bayes factor falls to 20 at a bias of 1.0098 and the worst-case Bayes factor falls to 1 at 1.559, so ω⋆=1.01\omega^\star = 1.01. With the memo at weight 10 the counts are 18 and 3, the two biases are 2.334 and 3.236, and ω⋆=2.33\omega^\star = 2.33. In the applications table, ω⋆\omega^\star now fills the column the separation used to fill. Figure 3 plots both biases against every weight on the memo from 1 to 20.

The coding analysis changed the same way (Paper/appendix.qmd, sec-sens-coding). The authors report the smallest number of re-codings at which either condition fails. The supplement’s code computes the worst-case half in an inline loop because the package does not provide it.

The worst-case Bayes factor takes stated weights on the working theory’s side

On 2026-08-30 the paper’s tests/bf_rescaled.R gained bounded_bf_rescaled(y_W, y_R, a1, b1). It computes the worst-case Bayes factor when the researcher states a Beta(a1,b1)(a_1, b_1) distribution rescaled onto the working theory’s shares instead of the uniform. Only the working theory’s weights enter, because the rival is evaluated at one half whatever weights the rival’s proponent might state. The replications’ sensitivity tables report it beside the uniform-weights value: at nine of twelve it is 2.07 under Beta(1/2, 1/2) and 4.38 under Beta(10, 10). The package’s bf_worst_case() took no weights.

One application was re-coded

On 2026-08-30 you moved Hammoud-Gallego and Freier from 10 observations for the working theory and 3 for the rival to 11 and 2 (commit 117e878), because their null result on emigrant numbers counts against a rival predictor. The uniform-weights Bayes factor rises from 33.86 to 153.57. The worst-case Bayes factor rises from 3.97 to 14.91. The number of re-codings that takes the uniform-weights value below 20 rises from one to two. tests/testthat/test-applications.R pinned the old counts.

The supplement has a finite-archive version of both Bayes factors

On 2026-09-11 Daniel added the section “Finite evidence without replacement” (Paper/appendix.qmd, lines 143–245). An archive holds MM documents, and KK of them support the working theory. The working theory claims K>M/2K > M/2 and the rival claims KK at most M/2M/2. The uniform-weights version averages the hypergeometric probability of the counts over each theory’s values of KK. The worst-case version evaluates the rival at the largest KK at or below M/2M/2. At nine of twelve drawn from an archive of 20, the uniform-weights version is 162.88. In every case the authors computed, whenever the binomial Bayes factors meet the rule, the finite ones meet it too. So a researcher need not choose MM, but may vary it as a sensitivity parameter. The finite-archive version is not the urn that bf_urn() computes, whose composition was built from the observed counts.

Two analyses the package offers are no longer in the paper

The whole-interval Beta(1,M+1)(1, M + 1) prior, where MM counts background cases favoring the rival rather than documents in an archive, was what sens_binomial() used for M_star and what the app drew in its second sensitivity plot. It now sits inside a commented block of the supplement (lines 465–532). The separated Bayes factor and its separation g*g^* are commented out of the supplement (lines 769–1062).

The paper dropped gendered pronouns

On 2026-08-30 you removed “she,” “her,” “he,” and “his” from both documents. The package’s help pages, README, vignette, and app used “she” for the researcher and “her” for the rival, on 221 lines.

Five worst-case cells in the supplement’s study tables

Each study’s subsection of the supplement has a table of Bayes factors under changed assumptions; for Andersen it is tbl-app-andersen-sens. The tables are built from replications/<study>/sensitivity_axes.csv. One row of each table varies the search bias over ω=1,2,5\omega = 1, 2, 5. In Andersen’s table the worst-case column of that row reads 2.73 / 0.67 / 0.28.

The 0.28 is not the worst case. Here is the arithmetic at Andersen’s counts, nine of twelve, and ω=5\omega = 5.

  • A search with bias ω\omega turns a share θ\theta of the evidence into a share q=ωθ/(ωθ+1−θ)q = \omega\theta/(\omega\theta + 1 - \theta) among the observations found. At ω=5\omega = 5 the rival’s share of one half becomes q=5/6=0.833q = 5/6 = 0.833. The probability of nine of twelve at q=0.833q = 0.833 is 0.197.
  • The rival claims every share at or below one half, not only one half. At θ=0.375\theta = 0.375 the same search gives q=1.875/2.5=0.75q = 1.875/2.5 = 0.75. The probability of nine of twelve at q=0.75q = 0.75 is 0.258. No share gives more, because nine of twelve is most probable when q=9/12q = 9/12.
  • The numerator, the working theory’s average, is 0.0554. The table divides it by 0.197 and prints 0.28. Divided by 0.258, the largest probability the rival’s shares can give, it is 0.21.

The paper defines the worst-case Bayes factor as the one whose denominator is the largest probability any weights on the rival’s shares can give. Without bias, and with at least as many observations for the working theory as for the rival, that denominator is the probability at one half. With bias it stays at one half only while ω/(1+ω)\omega/(1 + \omega), the share found when the rival’s share is one half, is at most k/Nk/N. The inequality ω/(1+ω)≤k/N\omega/(1 + \omega) \le k/N rearranges to ω≤k/r\omega \le k/r. At a larger bias the largest denominator is the probability at q=k/Nq = k/N.

Five printed cells are affected:

Study Counts ω\omega Printed At the rival’s best share
Andersen (9, 3) 5 0.28 0.21
Mor (8, 2) 5 0.41 0.40
Winward (14, 3) 5 0.38 0.37
Pavone and Stiansen (7, 4) 2 0.33 0.32
Pavone and Stiansen (7, 4) 5 0.18 0.05

Steinsson and Hammoud-Gallego and Freier are unaffected: Steinsson has no rival observations, and for Hammoud-Gallego and Freier k/r=11/2=5.5k/r = 11/2 = 5.5 is above 5.

None of the paper’s decisions or tipping points change. Every affected cell is below 1 under both computations, so a researcher following the rule keeps the rival there either way. And each bias at which the paper reports the worst-case value reaching 1 is below k/rk/r for its study: 1.56 against 3 for Andersen, 2.01 against 4 for Mor, 2.49 against 4.67 for Winward, and 2.81 against 5.5 for Hammoud-Gallego and Freier. That ordering holds for any counts. At the bias where ω/(1+ω)\omega/(1 + \omega) equals k/Nk/N, the denominator is the largest probability the counts can have at any share, and the numerator averages smaller probabilities, so the worst-case value is below 1 at that bias. It starts above 1 at ω=1\omega = 1 whenever the rule holds, so it reaches 1 at a smaller bias, where one half is still the rival’s best share.

On 2026-10-27 you chose to recompute the five cells at the rival’s best share and to add a note to the supplement saying why and how. Item 5 of the next section lists what that takes.

What the paper repository has to change once DrWrinch 0.0.2.1 is on GitHub

These edits belong to a session in ~/repos/fully_specified_bf. The first three are required: without them the paper, the supplement, or the replications stop with an error once the paper’s renv library installs the new version.

  1. tests/bf_weighted.R has two cross-checks guarded by requireNamespace("DrWrinch"). The one in binom_bf_weighted() calls DrWrinch::bf_binomial(W, R, omega = omega); replace that call with DrWrinch::bf_uniform_weights(W, R, omega = omega), which computes the same number. The one in hyper_bf_weighted() calls DrWrinch::bf_urn(); delete it, because the package no longer has the urn. Every file that sources tests/bf_weighted.R depends on this fix: Paper/evalues.qmd (chunk sensitivity-full), Paper/appendix.qmd (sec-sens-bias and the applications section), and the six replications/<study>/our_bf.R. Keep that cross-check’s tolerance of 1e-6. The package now integrates to a relative tolerance of 1e-10, while the paper’s own binom_bf_weighted() keeps R’s default, so any gap between the two comes from the paper’s side.
  2. Paper/appendix.qmd, sec-sens-coding: the chunk that defines coding_sens() calls sens_coding(k, r, model = "binomial", threshold = 20)$x_star, and sens_coding() no longer has a model argument. sens_coding(k, r)$x_star returns the smaller of the two tipping points, which is what coding_sens() computes, so the chunk can call it directly. The comment on library(DrWrinch) in the chunk sens-setup names bf_binomial and sens_binomial, which are gone.
  3. Paper/appendix.qmd, sec-reproduction: every call changes. bf_binomial(9, 3) becomes bf_uniform_weights(9, 3); source("../tests/bf_bounded.R") and bounded_bf(9, 3) become bf_worst_case(9, 3); sens_binomial(9, 3)$omega_star becomes sens_bias(9, 3)$omega_star, which now also asks when the worst-case value falls to 1 and still returns 1.0098 here; sens_coding(9, 3, model = "binomial", threshold = 20)$x_star becomes sens_coding(9, 3)$x_star; and the weighted calls at (18, 3) become bf_uniform_weights(18, 3) and bf_worst_case(18, 3). The prose names bf_binomial and tests/bf_bounded.R as the sources, lists “the separation” among the numbers reproduced, and sends readers to ?bf_binomial and ?sens_binomial; all of that changes with the calls. The TODO comment about renaming bf_binomial can go.
  4. renv.lock records DrWrinch 0.0.1.9001 from a local source. Install 0.0.2.1 from GitHub and snapshot.
  5. The five worst-case cells (previous section), recomputed with the rival at its best share, plus a note saying why and how:
    • In worst_bf_weighted() in tests/bf_weighted.R, divide by dbinom(W, N, min(omega / (1 + omega), W / N)) instead of dbinom(W, N, omega / (1 + omega)) when W >= R. Below ω=W/R\omega = W/R the two agree, so sens_bias_worst() and every tipping point the paper prints stay as they are. A cross-check against DrWrinch::bf_worst_case(W, R, omega = omega), guarded the way item 1’s is, would tie the two implementations together.
    • Rerun make replications, which rewrites the six sensitivity_axes.csv files. Andersen’s, Mor’s, and Winward’s change at ω=5\omega = 5, and Pavone and Stiansen’s at ω=2\omega = 2 and 5.
    • In sec-sens-bias of Paper/appendix.qmd, the formula for the worst-case Bayes factor under bias divides by q*k(1−q*)rq^{*k}(1 - q^*)^{r} with q*=min⁡(ω/(1+ω),k/N)q^* = \min(\omega/(1 + \omega), k/N) instead of by the same expression at q(1/2)=ω/(1+ω)q(1/2) = \omega/(1 + \omega).
    • The note, in sec-sens-bias with a pointer from each study table, says why: the worst-case Bayes factor divides by the largest probability the rival’s shares can give the counts; a biased search turns the rival’s shares into shares found of at most ω/(1+ω)\omega/(1 + \omega); the counts are most probable at a share found of k/Nk/N; so once ω\omega exceeds k/rk/r the rival’s best share is below one half. It gives Andersen’s arithmetic at ω=5\omega = 5 (0.0554 / 0.258 = 0.21 against 0.0554 / 0.197 = 0.28), and it says that no decision and no tipping point changes, because the worst-case value reaches 1 before ω\omega reaches k/rk/r.

Item 3 is on the path to the next arXiv replacement, not cleanup. The current preprint’s reproduction section calls bf_binomial(), sens_binomial(), and sens_coding(model = "binomial"), none of which exists once 0.0.2.1 is on GitHub, so a reader who installs the package to reproduce the preprint will meet errors until the replacement is posted.

Two things do not have to change. Paper/evalues.qmd sources tests/bf_bounded.R and tests/bf_rescaled.R and works unchanged once item 1 is done. This repository’s earlier plan proposed switching it to library(DrWrinch), but the paper project’s memory records your rule that the main paper’s body does not call DrWrinch, so the list leaves that switch out. And the replications still compute the urn’s Bayes factor (column hyper_bf) and the separation (separation_g), which no table prints; removing them is cleanup, not a fix.

Changes made without asking

  1. bf_worst_case() gains three arguments: omega for search bias, which matches bf_uniform_weights(omega = ), and a1, b1 for the working theory’s weights, which match bf_rescaled(). The closed form stays as the fast path at the defaults. Other values are integrated, as bf_binomial() integrated when omega was not 1.
  2. test-applications.R moves Hammoud-Gallego and Freier to (11, 2). It also pins each study’s ω⋆\omega^\star as the applications table reports it: 5.49, 1.74, 1.70, 1.14, and 1.01, no entry for Pavone and Stiansen, and 1.67 for Pavone and Stiansen with the letter at weight 10.
  3. New tests pin the numbers above. They also pin how bf_worst_case() treats bias: up to ω=k/r\omega = k/r it returns the paper’s value, with the rival at one half, and past that bias it returns the smallest value over the rival’s shares.
  4. The help pages, README, vignette, DESCRIPTION, and app state the paper’s rule and stop presenting the worst-case Bayes factor as an error rate at
    1. They drop the gendered pronouns by the four rules you used in the paper: drop the possessive, recast the sentence, use singular “they,” or name the role.
  5. The app takes two thresholds, 20 and 1, and says whether a researcher following the rule sets the rival aside. It reports ω⋆\omega^\star and the coding tipping point under the rule. The panel for the worst-case Bayes factor loses its separation line.
  6. The root finder behind sens_bias() uses the paper’s tolerance, so that its biases agree with the paper’s to six digits instead of four.
  7. The version moves from 0.0.2.0 to 0.0.2.1, and .dw_needed in inst/shiny/global.R moves with it.

This session did not change the paper repository. The section before this one lists the edits it needs.

Decisions

  1. Should the paper’s rule become the default in the sensitivity functions? I recommend yes. A new sens_bias(y_W, y_R, threshold_uniform = 20, threshold_worst = 1) would return the bias at which each condition fails and the smaller of the two. sens_coding() would take the same two thresholds and a new default, model = "rule", returning the number of re-codings at which each condition fails and the smaller of the two. model = "worst_case" would then return a tipping point at the worst-case threshold instead of the separation table. No code in either version of the paper calls that branch. The alternative leaves sens_coding() as it is and adds rule functions beside it. That alternative breaks nothing, but the package would then give two answers to the coding question.
  2. Should the package add the finite-archive Bayes factors? I recommend adding them, as bf_uniform_weights_finite(y_W, y_R, M) and bf_worst_case_finite(y_W, y_R, M), and rewording the deprecation notice of bf_urn() to point to them. That notice says the paper has no hypergeometric model. The supplement has had one since 2026-09-11.
  3. What should happen to M_star? I recommend deprecating sens_binomial() the way bf_urn() was deprecated: it keeps returning what it returns and warns once per session. sens_bias() would replace its omega_star, and its M_star belongs to an analysis the paper has commented out. The app’s background-cases plot would go. The supplement’s reproduction section still calls sens_binomial(), so the paper’s render would show the warning until the switch to library(DrWrinch) replaces that call.

Your answers, 2026-10-27

  1. The rule is the default. Because of answer 3, sens_coding() takes no model argument at all: like sens_bias(), it always returns the tipping point for each condition and the smaller of the two, so the separation table and the urn branch go with the functions behind them.
  2. Add bf_uniform_weights_finite() and bf_worst_case_finite().
  3. Drop rather than deprecate, since no one else uses the package. Dropped: bf_urn(), sens_urn(), the deprecation helper, sens_binomial() (its M_star and the app’s background-cases plot with it), bf_binomial() (with the whole-interval Beta prior and theta_cut), and the separated Bayes factor (bf_separated(), separation_g(), bf_separated_bias()). Anything the paper neither uses nor is likely to use goes too. BiasedUrn leaves Imports, because only bf_urn() needed it.
  4. Under bias, bf_worst_case() divides by the largest probability the rival’s shares can give the counts, and the paper recomputes its five affected cells the same way, with a note saying why and how. When the counts favor the rival (yW<yRy_W < y_R) the function keeps the rival at one half, as the paper’s closed form does for every count; the rule’s second condition fails at those counts under either convention.

Dropping bf_binomial() and bf_urn() breaks the two cross-checks in the paper’s tests/bf_weighted.R that call them through DrWrinch::, as soon as the paper’s renv library gets the new version. Item 1 of the section on the paper repository says how to fix each one.

Tests written before implementation

Rewritten: test-bf_uniform_weights.R, test-bf_worst_case.R, test-bf_rescaled.R, test-sens_coding.R, test-applications.R. New: test-bf_finite.R, test-sens_bias.R. Removed with the functions they tested: test-bf_binomial.R, test-bf_urn.R, test-sens.R, test-deprecated.R, setup-deprecation.R. The app’s four test files were rewritten after the functions passed their tests and before the app was changed: test-app_helpers.R (new helpers interpret_rule(), interpret_bias(), interpret_coding(), and a bf_omega_curve() that returns both Bayes factors), test-app_plots.R (one bias picture with two curves and the two thresholds), test-app_server.R (two threshold inputs, a rule card, no separation, no prior sweep), and test-app_decomposition.R (renamed from test-app_worst_case.R, with the separation tests removed).

The tests pin one behavior the memo did not anticipate. The finite-archive worst-case value is 0/0, and so NaN, when neither the working theory nor the half-split archive can produce the counts (no supporting document in a full reading of an archive of six). That happens only when the counts favor the rival.

Decision

The paper’s HANDOFF says Matias Lopez plans to submit by 2026-10-30. Should the paper-repository edits above be made before that submission? I recommend yes. The supplement’s reproduction section calls functions that are no longer on GitHub, so a reviewer who installs the package to reproduce the running example would meet errors, and the five worst-case cells would otherwise go out computed with the rival held at one half.
